title: The seven chakras, an overview
text: In Tantric and yogic tradition the chakras (wheels or lotuses) are described as energy centres along the spine, usually counted as seven: Muladhara (root), Svadhisthana (sacral), Manipura (navel), Anahata (heart), Vishuddha (throat), Ajna (between the brows) and Sahasrara (crown). Each is linked to a lotus with a set number of petals, a bija (seed) sound and an element. The classical description most often cited is the Shat-chakra-nirupana, a sixteenth-century Tantric text. Different lineages describe the details differently.

title: The rainbow chakra colours are a modern convention
text: The familiar scheme of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet for the seven chakras is a modern convention, popularised in the West during the twentieth century through Theosophical and New Age writing, and it is now common in yoga studios and wellness art. It is not found in the classical texts. The Shat-chakra-nirupana describes the lotuses and their regions in different colours. Pandit ji should therefore call the rainbow colours "the modern popular scheme", and never present them as ancient scripture.

title: Classical lotus colours in the Shat-chakra-nirupana
text: Translations of the Shat-chakra-nirupana, such as Arthur Avalon's "The Serpent Power", describe the lotuses in colours that do not match the rainbow scheme: for example a crimson Muladhara, a vermilion Svadhisthana, a dark, rain-cloud-coloured Manipura, a deep red Anahata, a smoky purple Vishuddha, a white Ajna and a shining white Sahasrara. Translators vary, and other Tantric texts give other schemes. These are described as meditation images, and a reviewer should check the wording against a trusted translation before use.

title: Muladhara, the root chakra
text: Muladhara ("root support") is traditionally placed at the base of the spine. Its element is earth (prithvi), its bija sound is LAM, and its lotus has four petals. The modern popular colour is red. In yogic tradition it is linked with stability, groundedness and the dormant Kundalini energy, which is said to rest here. In some traditions Ganesha is associated with this centre, and the Ganapati Atharvashirsha refers to him dwelling at the Muladhara. Descriptions vary by lineage.

title: Svadhisthana, the sacral chakra
text: Svadhisthana ("one's own abode") is traditionally placed at the root of the genitals or low in the abdomen. Its element is water (apas), its bija sound is VAM, and its lotus has six petals. The modern popular colour is orange. In yogic tradition it is linked with creativity, pleasure, flow and emotion. Systems differ about its exact location, and some texts give different deities for it. The colour stated here is the modern convention, not the classical one.

title: Manipura, the solar plexus chakra
text: Manipura ("city of jewels") is traditionally placed at the navel. Its element is fire (agni), its bija sound is RAM, and its lotus has ten petals. The modern popular colour is yellow. In yogic tradition it is linked with willpower, digestion, confidence and inner heat (tejas). Some modern writers connect it with the Sun, which matches the fire element, though that link is a popular association rather than a fixed rule. Lineages differ in their descriptions.

title: Anahata, the heart chakra
text: Anahata ("unstruck") is traditionally placed at the centre of the chest, at the heart. Its element is air (vayu), its bija sound is YAM, and its lotus has twelve petals. The modern popular colour is green. The name refers to the "unstruck sound", an inner sound that arises without any two things striking. In yogic tradition it is linked with love, compassion and devotion (bhakti). Some traditions place the Ishta Devata, one's chosen deity, here for meditation.

title: Vishuddha, the throat chakra
text: Vishuddha ("especially pure") is traditionally placed at the throat. Its element is ether or space (akasha), its bija sound is HAM, and its lotus has sixteen petals, linked in tradition with the sixteen Sanskrit vowels. The modern popular colour is blue, sometimes light blue. In yogic tradition it is linked with speech, truth and expression, and with chanting. The throat is also where Shiva is said to hold the Halahala poison as Neelkantha, though that is a Puranic story, not a chakra text.

title: Ajna, the third-eye chakra
text: Ajna ("command") is traditionally placed between the eyebrows, the spot of the tilak or bindi. Its bija sound is OM, and its lotus has two petals. It is not linked to one of the five elements in most descriptions, but to mind and awareness. The modern popular colour is indigo. In yogic tradition it is linked with insight and focus, and the third eye of Shiva is a related image in devotion. Texts differ about the details.

title: Sahasrara, the crown chakra
text: Sahasrara ("thousand-petalled") is traditionally placed at the crown of the head or just above it. It is described as a lotus of a thousand petals and is linked with the highest state of union, often described as Shiva (consciousness) meeting Shakti (energy). It has no element, and its sound is Om or silence in many descriptions. The modern popular colour is violet or white. Practitioners describe it as a goal of meditation, and it is not an organ or something to be measured.

title: The bija mantras of the seven chakras
text: The bija (seed) sounds commonly given are LAM for Muladhara, VAM for Svadhisthana, RAM for Manipura, YAM for Anahata, HAM for Vishuddha and OM for Ajna, with Sahasrara linked to Om or silence. In yoga classes they are chanted in sequence, each held at the relevant part of the body. The sounds come from Tantric texts and teachers, and different lineages teach different practices. Chanting is a contemplative practice, not a medical treatment.

title: Chakra T-shirt designs and what they depict
text: Chakra T-shirt designs usually show seven lotuses or circles along a spine, in rainbow colours with a bija sound in Devanagari. Pandit ji can describe these as meditation imagery based on yogic tradition, with the rainbow colours as a modern style. A chakra design may be suggested to someone interested in yoga or meditation, and it is a symbol to wear, not a treatment. Using the classical colours or a single lotus is also a valid design choice.

title: Shiva, iconography and symbols
text: Shiva is worshipped as the great ascetic and the lord of Kailash. Common iconography shows a third eye on the forehead, a crescent moon and the river Ganga in his matted locks, a serpent around his neck, ash on his body, a trishul (trident) and a damru (small drum). His vahana (vehicle) is Nandi the bull. He is worshipped most often as the aniconic Shivling. The Shiva Purana is the text most associated with his worship, and Shiva is also revered in the Vedic Rudram hymn. Shaiva traditions differ between regions.

title: Shiva, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Shiva is traditionally worshipped on Mondays, on Pradosh (the twilight of the thirteenth lunar day), and during the month of Shravan. Maha Shivaratri is his major festival. Devotees offer water, milk, bael leaves and white flowers, and often wear white or ash-grey. Well-known mantras are "Om Namah Shivaya", the Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra and the Shiva Panchakshara Stotra. Some South Indian traditions also observe Monday, and Shaiva communities differ in their rituals.

title: Parvati (Gauri), iconography and symbols
text: Parvati, the daughter of the mountain king Himavan, is the consort of Shiva and the mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. She is shown as a gentle, graceful goddess, often seated beside Shiva, sometimes holding a lotus, and is also called Gauri, Uma and Shakti. She is regarded in Shakta tradition as an aspect of the Mother Goddess, and her fierce forms include Durga. The Shiva Purana tells of her penance to win Shiva as her husband.

title: Parvati, festivals, colours and mantras
text: Parvati as Gauri is worshipped in festivals such as Hartalika Teej, Gangaur in Rajasthan and Gauri Puja, which are particularly observed by women for marital happiness in a devotional sense. Red, green and yellow are commonly worn at these festivals, with green especially popular in Teej. Gauri is also honoured on Mondays together with Shiva, and during Navratri as part of the Goddess. A commonly used mantra is "Om Gauryai Namah". Customs differ widely between regions and families.

title: Ganesha, iconography and symbols
text: Ganesha, the son of Shiva and Parvati, is shown with an elephant head, a large belly, one tusk broken or whole, and usually four arms. He commonly holds a pasha (noose), an ankusha (goad), a modak sweet and a broken tusk or lotus. His vahana is the mooshak, a mouse. The elephant head is read by devotees as a symbol of wisdom and a large capacity to listen; the mouse as the mastery of small desires. He is Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles, and is invoked first in most Hindu rites.

title: Ganesha, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Ganesha is traditionally worshipped on Wednesdays, and on Chaturthi (the fourth lunar day) each month; Sankashti Chaturthi after the full moon is widely kept, and in Maharashtra the Tuesday Sankashti is called Angarki. Ganesh Chaturthi is his major festival. Red, orange, yellow and green are commonly used; offerings include modak, durva grass and red hibiscus. Well-known mantras are "Om Gan Ganapataye Namah" and "Vakratunda Mahakaya". The Ganapati Atharvashirsha is the text associated with his worship. Practice varies by region.

title: Vishnu, iconography and symbols
text: Vishnu, the preserver in the Hindu trinity, is shown with blue skin, four arms and a crown, holding a shankh (conch), the Sudarshan Chakra (discus), a gada (mace) and a padma (lotus). He reclines on the serpent Sheshnag in the cosmic ocean, with Lakshmi at his feet, or rides Garuda the eagle. Tradition describes ten principal avatars (Dashavatara), including Rama and Krishna. Vaishnava traditions across India worship him under many names, such as Narayana, Hari and Venkateswara.

title: Vishnu, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Vishnu is traditionally worshipped on Thursdays and on Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day, which many Vaishnavas observe with a fast. Yellow, the colour of his pitambar (yellow cloth), and saffron are commonly used, with tulsi leaves as a key offering. Well-known mantras are "Om Namo Narayanaya" and "Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya", and the Vishnu Sahasranama is widely recited. Major observances include Vaikuntha Ekadashi and Devshayani Ekadashi. Practice varies among Vaishnava communities.

title: Krishna, iconography and symbols
text: Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, is shown with dark or blue skin, a peacock feather in his crown, a flute (bansuri), a yellow dhoti and often with cows or as a butter-loving child (Bal Gopal). He appears in the Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana, and the Bhagavad Gita records his teaching to Arjuna. Radha is commonly shown with him in devotional traditions. The flute is read by devotees as a symbol of the soul's call to the divine.

title: Krishna, festivals, colours and mantras
text: Krishna is celebrated at Janmashtami, his birth festival, and at Holi, Govardhan Puja and Radhashtami in many regions. Yellow and blue are commonly worn, as is peacock-feather imagery. Many devotees also keep Ekadashi. Well-known mantras include the Hare Krishna Maha Mantra and "Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya". Krishna bhakti has many streams, such as Vallabha, Gaudiya and Pushtimarg, with differing customs. He has no single fixed weekday.

title: Rama, iconography and symbols
text: Rama, an avatar of Vishnu and the hero of the Ramayana of Valmiki, is shown with blue or dark skin, a bow (kodanda) and arrows, usually with Sita and Lakshmana, and with Hanuman kneeling at his feet. He is called Maryada Purushottam, the ideal of dharma and duty. The Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas is the best-known retelling in much of North India. Rama's capital is traditionally Ayodhya. His dynasty is the Suryavansha, the solar line.

title: Rama, festivals, colours and mantras
text: Rama is celebrated at Ram Navami, and the story of his return to Ayodhya is marked at Diwali and Dussehra, with Ramlila performances in many towns. Saffron, yellow and blue are common colours. A well-loved chant is "Shri Ram Jai Ram Jai Jai Ram", and "Jai Shri Ram" is a common greeting; the Ram Raksha Stotra is also widely recited. Rama has no single fixed weekday, and many families also honour him on Thursdays or Tuesdays alongside Hanuman, depending on custom.

title: Hanuman, iconography and symbols
text: Hanuman, the devoted servant of Rama, is shown as a powerful monkey-faced figure, often red or vermilion in colour, carrying a gada (mace) and sometimes the Sanjeevani mountain. A popular image shows him tearing open his chest to reveal Rama and Sita in his heart. The Hanuman Chalisa, a forty-verse hymn by Tulsidas, praises his strength, devotion and humility. He is regarded as a son of Vayu, the wind god, and as a Chiranjivi, one who lives forever.

title: Hanuman, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Hanuman is traditionally worshipped on Tuesdays and Saturdays. His main festival is Hanuman Jayanti, observed on Chaitra Purnima in most of North India, while some regions, such as Tamil Nadu and Kerala, observe it at different dates. Red, orange and saffron are commonly used, with sindoor and jasmine oil offered at many temples. Common mantras include "Om Hanumate Namah" and "Jai Shri Ram". Reciting the Hanuman Chalisa is the most widespread practice.

title: Lakshmi, iconography and symbols
text: Lakshmi, the consort of Vishnu, is the goddess of wealth, prosperity and good fortune. She is shown seated or standing on a lotus, with gold coins pouring from one hand, and often flanked by two elephants (Gaja Lakshmi). Her vahana is the owl in many depictions. Tradition names eight forms called Ashta Lakshmi. The Sri Suktam is the Vedic hymn most associated with her. Her symbols are read by devotees as prosperity, purity and generosity, not only as material wealth.

title: Lakshmi, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Lakshmi is traditionally worshipped on Fridays, and especially on Diwali night (Lakshmi Puja). Other observances include Sharad Purnima, Varalakshmi Vratam in South India and Dhanteras. Red, pink, gold and white are commonly used, with red and gold favoured on Diwali. Well-known mantras are "Om Shreem Mahalakshmyai Namah" and the Mahalakshmi Ashtakam. Many homes light lamps and keep the entrance clean for her. Customs vary between regions.

title: Saraswati, iconography and symbols
text: Saraswati is the goddess of knowledge, music, speech and the arts. She is shown in white, seated on a white lotus or riding a hamsa (swan), holding a veena (stringed instrument), a book and a mala (rosary). The swan is read by devotees as the ability to discern truth, as the legend says it separates milk from water. Saraswati is also a sacred river in the Rigveda. Students and artists often keep her image near their books and instruments.

title: Saraswati, festivals, colours and mantras
text: Saraswati is celebrated at Vasant Panchami, in January or February, with yellow clothes and offerings, and during Navratri, especially in the South and in Bengal as Saraswati Puja on the last days. Many families perform Vidyarambham, a child's first writing, in her name. White and yellow are commonly used. A well-known mantra is "Om Aim Saraswatyai Namah". Some families link Wednesdays or Thursdays with her, but there is no single fixed day.

title: Durga, iconography and symbols
text: Durga is the warrior form of the Divine Mother. She is shown with ten arms holding weapons given by the gods, such as a trident, a discus, a sword and a bow, riding a lion or tiger. The Devi Mahatmya, also called the Durga Saptashati and part of the Markandeya Purana, narrates her victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Devotees read the image as the triumph of good over evil and as protection of dharma. Regional forms include Vaishno Devi and Ambaji.

title: Durga, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Durga is traditionally worshipped on Tuesdays and Fridays, on Ashtami, and during Navratri and Durga Puja. Red is the most common colour, with orange and yellow also popular. Well-known mantras are "Om Dum Durgayai Namah" and the Navarna mantra "Om Aim Hreem Kleem Chamundayai Vichche". Reciting the Durga Saptashati, Durga Chalisa or Durga Kavach is customary. Bengal, Gujarat and other regions each have their own style of celebration.

title: Kali, iconography and symbols
text: Kali is a form of the Mother Goddess, shown with dark skin, a garland of skulls or heads, a sword, a severed head and a lolling tongue, standing on Shiva. She is worshipped in Shakta tradition, especially in Bengal, Assam and Odisha, and at Kalighat in Kolkata. Devotional poets such as Ramprasad Sen sang to her as a loving mother. Devotees read her fierce image as the power of time and the destruction of ego and illusion, not as a figure of ill will. Interpretations differ between schools.

title: Kali, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Kali is traditionally worshipped on Amavasya (new moon) nights, and Kali Puja is celebrated in Bengal on the new moon of the Diwali period. She is also worshipped during Navratri and by some on Tuesdays and Fridays. Black, red and deep blue are commonly used, with red hibiscus as a traditional offering. A well-known mantra is "Om Kreem Kalikayai Namah". Her worship has distinct regional and lineage rules, so a family's own tradition or priest is the best guide.

title: Surya Dev, iconography and symbols
text: Surya, the Sun god, is shown standing or riding a chariot drawn by seven horses, driven by the charioteer Aruna, and holding lotus flowers in his hands. The seven horses are often read as the seven days of the week or the seven colours of light. The famous Sun Temple at Konark in Odisha is built as a giant chariot. Surya is honoured as the visible deity, whose daily rising can be seen by all, and the Gayatri Mantra is addressed to him as Savitr.

title: Surya, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Surya is traditionally worshipped on Sundays, at sunrise. Observances include Makar Sankranti, Ratha Saptami and Chhath Puja, in which devotees offer arghya to the setting and rising Sun. Red, orange and saffron are commonly used, with red flowers and water offered in a copper vessel. Well-known mantras include "Om Suryaya Namah" and the Aditya Hridayam. Sun worship is also central to Surya Namaskar practice. Customs differ by region, with Bihar and Jharkhand especially known for Chhath.

title: Shani Dev, iconography and symbols
text: Shani Dev is the deity of the graha Saturn. He is shown with dark skin, wearing black or dark blue, carrying a bow or a trident, and riding a crow or vulture. Puranic tradition describes him as a son of Surya and Chhaya, and as a god of justice who is believed to give results according to one's karma. Well-known temples include Shani Shingnapur in Maharashtra and Thirunallar in Tamil Nadu. Devotees are encouraged to see him as a stern teacher rather than a figure to fear.

title: Shani Dev, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Shani Dev is traditionally worshipped on Saturdays, on Shani Amavasya (a Saturday new moon) and on Shani Jayanti, his birth festival on the new moon of the Jyeshtha month in many calendars. Black and dark blue are commonly used, with mustard oil, sesame and iron items as offerings. A well-known mantra is "Om Sham Shanaishcharaya Namah". Many also recite the Hanuman Chalisa on Saturdays. Customs vary by region and family.

title: Kartikeya (Murugan), iconography and symbols
text: Kartikeya, also called Skanda, Murugan, Subramanya and Kumara, is the son of Shiva and Parvati and the commander of the divine army. He is shown as a youthful warrior with a vel (spear), riding a peacock, and in some forms with six faces (Shanmukha). He is especially beloved in Tamil Nadu, where he is the chief deity of the Tamil people, and also worshipped in Karnataka, Kerala and Maharashtra. The peacock is read as the taming of pride.

title: Kartikeya, days, colours, festivals and mantras
text: Kartikeya is traditionally worshipped on Tuesdays, on Shashti (the sixth lunar day) and at festivals such as Skanda Shashti, Thaipusam and Panguni Uthiram, mainly in the South and among the Tamil diaspora. Red, orange and yellow are commonly used. Well-known chants include "Om Saravana Bhava" and "Om Shanmukhaya Namah". Pilgrimage to the six major Murugan temples (Arupadai Veedu) is a notable devotional tradition. Practice varies by region and community.

title: Santoshi Maa, iconography and symbols
text: Santoshi Maa is a goddess of contentment and satisfaction, shown as a gentle goddess seated on a lotus, holding a sword or trident and a kalash or bowl. In popular tradition she is a daughter of Ganesha. Her devotion is not described in the older Puranas and became widespread in North India in the second half of the twentieth century, helped by the 1975 film "Jai Santoshi Maa". She is mainly worshipped by women in North and Central India.

title: Santoshi Maa, vrat, colours and offerings
text: Santoshi Maa is traditionally worshipped on Fridays. Her best-known vrat is kept for sixteen consecutive Fridays, ending with a udyapan (concluding ceremony). The offering is gur (jaggery) and roasted chana (gram), and many observers avoid sour foods during the fast. Saffron, yellow and red are commonly seen in her imagery. The Santoshi Maa Vrat Katha is read, and a simple mantra is "Om Shri Santoshi Matre Namah". Customs vary by family and region.

title: How doshas are described in Jyotish
text: In Jyotish a dosha is a planetary configuration that astrologers describe as carrying challenges, and tradition also lists remedies (upaya) such as prayer, charity and ritual. Astrologers differ widely on which doshas exist, how a chart is read, and how much weight to give them, and many stress that a full chart has other supportive factors. Pandit ji should describe doshas as what tradition says, invite the person to consult a qualified astrologer, and avoid fear language or any claim that a remedy changes an outcome.

title: Mangal Dosha (Manglik), what tradition says
text: Mangal Dosha, also called Kuja Dosha or being "Manglik", is said in Jyotish to arise when Mars is placed in certain houses of the birth chart, most often the first, fourth, seventh, eighth or twelfth, and in some schools the second. It is mainly discussed in connection with marriage compatibility. Tradition also lists cancelling conditions, for example when both partners are Manglik or when Mars is in its own or exalted sign. Because many charts are said to qualify, astrologers differ about how much weight it deserves.

title: Mangal Dosha, traditionally prescribed practices
text: Practices traditionally linked with Mangal Dosha include Tuesday worship of Hanuman, reciting the Hanuman Chalisa, a Mangal Shanti puja (often at the Mangalnath temple in Ujjain), keeping a Tuesday fast, offering red lentils and jaggery in charity, and chanting the Mangal beej mantra. In some regions a symbolic Kumbh Vivah is done. Families choose among these according to their tradition, and astrologers differ on what is advisable. These are customs, not treatments, and no outcome is promised.

title: Kaal Sarp Dosh, what tradition says
text: Kaal Sarp Dosh is said to occur when all seven classical planets lie on one side of the Rahu-Ketu axis in a birth chart. Modern astrologers list twelve types, named for the house of Rahu, such as Anant, Kulik, Vasuki, Shankhpal, Padma, Mahapadma, Takshak, Karkotak, Shankhchud, Ghatak, Vishdhar and Sheshnag. The concept is not found in Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra and is considered by some astrologers a later, modern addition, while others follow it closely. Opinions differ, and it should be described as a debated tradition.

title: Kaal Sarp Dosh, traditionally prescribed practices
text: Practices linked with Kaal Sarp Dosh include a Kaal Sarp puja at places like Trimbakeshwar, Ujjain or Srikalahasti, worship of Shiva with Rudrabhishek, honouring Nag (serpent) deities on Nag Panchami, chanting the Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra and giving a pair of silver serpents in ritual. Some devotees also visit the Shiva temple on Mondays. These are traditions followed by some families, and no result is promised.

title: Sade Sati, what it means in Jyotish
text: Sade Sati ("seven and a half") is the period of about seven and a half years when Saturn passes through three zodiac signs: the one before the Moon's sign in a person's birth chart, the Moon's own sign, and the one after it. Each sign takes about two and a half years, and it happens roughly every thirty years since Saturn takes about 29 years to circle the zodiac. Many astrologers describe it as a period of testing, discipline and slow progress, and effects are said to depend on the whole chart.

title: Shani Dhaiya (Small Panoti)
text: Shani Dhaiya, also called Small Panoti or Ashtama and Kantak Shani, is the period of about two and a half years when Saturn passes through the fourth or eighth sign from the Moon's birth sign. Astrologers describe it as a period for patience and care in decisions, and views on its effects vary a great deal between schools. As with Sade Sati, the result is said to depend on the full chart. Many people observe it by prayers to Shani Dev, which is a personal choice.

title: Sade Sati, traditionally observed practices
text: During Sade Sati, devotees traditionally worship Shani Dev and Hanuman on Saturdays, light a sesame or mustard oil lamp, reciting the Shani Chalisa or Hanuman Chalisa, give sesame, black cloth or oil to those in need, and serve the elderly and workers. Some visit Shani temples such as Shingnapur. The tradition presents Shani as a fair teacher of karma, so honest work and kindness are considered part of the practice. These are customs, not promised remedies.

title: Pitra Dosha, what tradition says
text: Pitra Dosha is a term used by some astrologers for an afflicted placement of the Sun or the ninth house of a birth chart, which they link with the family's duties to its ancestors (pitras). Tradition teaches that remembering ancestors with shraddha and tarpan is a duty of gratitude. The concept is a later development and astrologers differ on it. It is best presented as an invitation to honour one's ancestors and not as a cause for worry.

title: Pitra Dosha, traditionally observed practices
text: Practices linked with honouring ancestors include shraddha and tarpan during Pitru Paksha, especially on Sarva Pitru Amavasya, pind daan at Gaya, feeding Brahmins, cows, crows and dogs, giving to the needy, planting a peepal tree and offering water to the Sun. Some families also read the Bhagavad Gita during this period. These are acts of remembrance, and families follow them as their custom and means allow.

title: Maha Shivaratri
text: Maha Shivaratri, the "great night of Shiva", falls on the fourteenth lunar night of the dark half of the month of Phalguna (Magha by the North Indian purnimanta count), usually in February or March. Devotees fast, keep a night-long vigil (jagran), bathe the Shivling with milk, water and honey, offer bael leaves and chant "Om Namah Shivaya". Tradition describes it as the night of Shiva's marriage to Parvati in some regions, and as the night of the Lingodbhava, the pillar of light, in others. White is commonly worn, with no strict rule.

title: Shravan Somvar, the Mondays of Shravan
text: Shravan (also called Sawan) is a monsoon month, around July and August, that is especially dear to Shiva, and its Mondays (Shravan Somvar) are observed with fasts and Shivling abhishek. In North India many pilgrims make the Kanwar Yatra, carrying Ganga water to Shiva temples. White is a common colour, and green, linked to the rains, is also widely worn in the month in North India. The dates of the month differ between the North (purnimanta) and South or West (amanta) calendars, so the exact weeks vary by region.

title: Navratri, the two main Navratris
text: Navratri means "nine nights" and is the festival of the Goddess. Two are widely celebrated: Chaitra Navratri in March or April, which ends with Ram Navami, and Sharad Navratri in September or October, the best known, ending with Vijayadashami (Dussehra). Two further Gupt (hidden) Navratris occur in other months. Devotees fast, worship Durga in nine forms, and read the Durga Saptashati. Garba and dandiya are performed in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, and doll displays called Golu in parts of South India.

title: Chaitra Navratri
text: Chaitra Navratri begins on the first day of the Hindu lunar year in the month of Chaitra, which is the new year in many North and Central Indian calendars (celebrated as Ugadi and Gudi Padwa in the Deccan). Families set up a kalash (Ghatasthapana), sow barley seeds, fast, and worship the nine forms of the Goddess. The ninth day is Ram Navami, the birth of Rama. In many families, the colour red or orange is worn. Customs vary between regions.

title: Sharad Navratri and Vijayadashami
text: Sharad Navratri, in the month of Ashwin, is the principal nine-night festival of the Goddess. In Gujarat it is marked by garba and dandiya, in Bengal by Durga Puja from the sixth to tenth day, and in many northern towns by Ramlila performances that end with Dussehra, when effigies of Ravana are burnt. In the South, Saraswati Puja and Ayudha Puja fall on the last days. Many devotees fast for nine days and wear the day's colour. Practices vary widely.

title: The nine forms of Durga worshipped in Navratri
text: During Navratri, one form of the Goddess is worshipped each day in a common North Indian scheme: Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri and Siddhidatri. Shailaputri is the daughter of the mountain, Brahmacharini the ascetic, Skandamata the mother of Kartikeya, and Mahagauri the radiant white form. The names are given in a verse traditionally recited in the Devi Kavacha. Some regions follow other sequences, so order and emphasis vary.

title: Navratri day colours, a modern popular custom
text: Wearing a different colour on each of the nine nights of Navratri is a modern popular custom, widely published in newspapers and on social media, and especially followed in Maharashtra, Gujarat and online. The colour usually follows the weekday on which each night falls, for example white on Monday, red on Tuesday, blue on Wednesday, yellow on Thursday, green on Friday, grey on Saturday and orange on Sunday. Lists differ between sources and years, and are not found in the classical texts. Many families simply wear red or any bright colour.

title: Diwali, the five days
text: Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated over five days around October or November: Dhanteras (worship of Dhanvantari and Lakshmi, with metal purchases), Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi Puja on the new moon night, Govardhan Puja and Annakut, and Bhai Dooj. The reason for celebrating varies: return of Rama to Ayodhya in much of North India, Krishna's victory over Narakasura in the South, and Lakshmi's worship in many homes. Lamps (diyas), rangoli and new clothes are customary, with red, gold and yellow common.

title: Diwali Lakshmi Puja
text: On the new moon night of Diwali, many homes worship Lakshmi together with Ganesha during the evening Pradosh period, using lamps, flowers, sweets and coins, and keep the entrance lit. Business families perform Chopda Pujan on new account books, and Kuber is also invoked. The timing is set each year by the panchang. In Bengal and Odisha the same night is Kali Puja. The colour most worn is red or gold, and customs vary by region.

title: Ganesh Chaturthi
text: Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birth of Ganesha on the fourth day of the bright half of Bhadrapada, around August or September. Clay idols are installed in homes and community pandals for one and a half, three, five, seven or ten days and immersed on Anant Chaturdashi. It is especially grand in Maharashtra, where Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped make it a public festival in the 1890s, and in Goa, Karnataka and Andhra. Modak is the favourite offering. Red, yellow and orange are commonly worn.

title: Hanuman Jayanti
text: Hanuman Jayanti marks the birth of Hanuman and is observed on Chaitra Purnima in most of North India, around March or April. Devotees visit temples before dawn, offer sindoor, red flowers and boondi, and recite the Hanuman Chalisa or Sundarkand. Other regions celebrate on different dates, for example in Tamil Nadu in the month of Margazhi, and in Andhra and Telangana at other times of the year. Red, orange and saffron are commonly worn. Dates vary by tradition.

title: Krishna Janmashtami
text: Janmashtami marks the birth of Krishna on the eighth day of the dark half of Bhadrapada (Shravana by the amanta calendar), around August or September, with the birth celebrated at midnight. Devotees fast until midnight, decorate cradles and tableaux (jhankis), sing bhajans and share butter and sweets. In Maharashtra, human pyramids break hanging pots in Dahi Handi. Yellow, blue and peacock shades are commonly worn. Vaishnava and Smarta traditions sometimes celebrate on different days, so dates differ.

title: Ram Navami
text: Ram Navami celebrates the birth of Rama on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra, around March or April, which is also the last day of Chaitra Navratri. Tradition places the birth at midday, and temples perform special aartis then. Devotees fast, read the Ramayana or Ramcharitmanas, and in Ayodhya large fairs are held. Panakam and kosambari are offered in the South. Saffron, yellow and light blue are commonly seen. Customs vary across regions.

title: Makar Sankranti
text: Makar Sankranti marks the day the Sun enters Makara (Capricorn) around 14 or 15 January, and the start of Uttarayan, the Sun's northward journey. It is celebrated as Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Maghi in Punjab, the day after Lohri, Magh Bihu in Assam and with kite flying in Gujarat. Devotees take holy dips, honour Surya and share til-gud (sesame and jaggery). In Maharashtra black clothes are customarily worn on this day, and yellow, orange and red are common elsewhere.

title: Vasant Panchami
text: Vasant Panchami falls on the fifth day of the bright half of Magha, around late January or February, and marks the arrival of spring. It is the main festival of Saraswati, whose worship includes placing books, pens and instruments before her image. Yellow is the traditional colour, in clothes and in food such as sweet yellow rice, linked with blooming mustard fields. Many families do Vidyarambh, the child's first writing, on this day. Kite flying is popular in Punjab and Haryana.

title: Karva Chauth
text: Karva Chauth is observed on the fourth day after the full moon in the month of Kartik, mainly in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. Married women fast from sunrise until moonrise, traditionally for the wellbeing and long life of their husbands, and then break the fast after seeing the moon through a sieve. The day includes worship of Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha and a Karva Chauth katha. Red, maroon and bridal colours are customary. Some husbands and unmarried women also fast now.

title: Chhath Puja
text: Chhath is a four-day festival of Surya and Chhathi Maiya, observed on the sixth day of the bright half of Kartik, about six days after Diwali, mainly in Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Nepal. Devotees fast for about thirty-six hours without water, stand in a river or pond and offer arghya to the setting Sun and to the rising Sun the next morning. Thekua and fruits are offered in bamboo baskets. Women often wear orange sindoor and bright saris. The festival is a distinctive regional tradition.

title: Dussehra (Vijayadashami)
text: Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, falls on the tenth day after the start of Sharad Navratri. In North India it commemorates Rama's victory over Ravana, marked by Ramlila and burning effigies of Ravana. In Bengal and the East it marks the end of Durga Puja, with idol immersion. In Karnataka, Mysuru's Dasara is a royal tradition, and in many places tools, vehicles and books are worshipped (Ayudha Puja). It is considered an auspicious day for starting learning or new ventures in many families. Customs vary.

title: Holi
text: Holi, the festival of colours, falls on the full moon of Phalguna (February or March). On the evening before, Holika Dahan, bonfires recall the story of Prahlad, who was devoted to Vishnu and survived the fire that burned his aunt Holika. The next day people play with coloured powders, and in Mathura and Vrindavan it is also linked to Krishna and Radha. White clothing is worn to show the colours. Regional versions include Lathmar Holi, Dol Jatra and Shigmo.

title: The Navagraha, nine grahas of Vedic astrology
text: The Navagraha are the nine "grahas" (literally "those that seize" or influences) of Jyotish, Vedic astrology: Surya (Sun), Chandra (Moon), Mangal (Mars), Budh (Mercury), Guru or Brihaspati (Jupiter), Shukra (Venus), Shani (Saturn), and the two shadow points Rahu and Ketu. Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra is the classical text most widely cited for their significations. Seven of them give their names to the days of the week. Many Hindu temples have a Navagraha shrine, and devotees often circle it after the main deity. Colours, grains, metals and gems linked to each graha vary somewhat between traditions.

title: Commonly given colours for the nine grahas
text: In many panchang and temple traditions the grahas are linked to colours as follows: Surya with red, orange or saffron; Chandra with white or cream; Mangal with red; Budh with green; Guru with yellow; Shukra with white, cream or soft pastel shades; Shani with black or dark blue; Rahu with smoky or dark blue-grey; Ketu with grey, brown or multicoloured. Lists differ by region and family, and some priests give slightly different shades. These are customs for what to wear or offer on a given day, and devotees follow them according to their own family practice.

title: Surya (Sun) in Vedic astrology
text: Surya, the Sun, is described in Jyotish as the "atma karaka", the significator of the soul or self, and is linked with vitality, authority, the father and leadership. Its day is Sunday (Ravivar). Commonly linked colours are red, orange and saffron; the metal is usually copper or gold; the grain is wheat; the gem is ruby (manik). Surya is worshipped as the visible deity of light. Interpretations differ among astrologers, and these associations describe what the tradition holds, not a prediction for any individual.

title: Surya worship practices and beej mantra
text: Devotees traditionally offer water (arghya) to the rising Sun, often in a copper vessel, while reciting Surya mantras. The beej (seed) mantra commonly given is "Om Hraam Hreem Hraum Sah Suryaya Namah". Other well-known practices are Surya Namaskar, the Gayatri Mantra addressed to the Sun as Savitr, and reading the Aditya Hridayam, a hymn to Surya that appears in the Ramayana. Many families keep Sunday observances such as eating simply and avoiding salt, though custom varies.

title: Chandra (Moon) in Vedic astrology
text: Chandra, the Moon, is linked in Jyotish with the mind (manas), emotions, mother and nourishment. Its day is Monday (Somvar). Commonly given colours are white and cream; the metal is silver; the grain is rice; the gem is pearl (moti). Shiva, who wears the crescent moon on his head, is the deity most often connected with Monday and the Moon. The Moon's phases are also the basis of the lunar calendar that sets many Hindu festivals. These are traditional associations, and astrologers differ on details.

title: Chandra worship practices and beej mantra
text: Monday observances for Chandra overlap with Shiva worship: many devotees fast on Mondays (Somvar vrat), offer water or milk to the Shivling, and wear white. The beej mantra commonly given is "Om Shraam Shreem Shraum Sah Chandraya Namah". Purnima (full moon) and Pradosh evenings are also considered auspicious times for Moon and Shiva worship. Whether a person follows these customs depends on family tradition, and practices differ between regions.

title: Mangal (Mars) in Vedic astrology
text: Mangal, Mars, is linked in Jyotish with courage, energy, siblings, land and the warrior spirit. Its day is Tuesday (Mangalvar). Commonly given colours are red and vermilion; the metal is copper; the grain is red lentil (masoor) or toor dal depending on region; the gem is red coral (moonga). Hanuman is the deity most commonly worshipped on Tuesdays in North India, and Kartikeya (Murugan) is also linked with Mangal, especially in the South. These are traditional associations and astrologers hold varying views.

title: Mangal worship practices and beej mantra
text: On Tuesdays many devotees visit a Hanuman temple, offer red flowers or sindoor, light a lamp and recite the Hanuman Chalisa. Some keep a Tuesday fast (Mangalvar vrat). The beej mantra commonly given for Mangal is "Om Kraam Kreem Kraum Sah Bhaumaya Namah". In Tamil Nadu, Tuesdays are also observed for Murugan and for Amman temples. Practices differ by family and region, and none is required.

title: Budh (Mercury) in Vedic astrology
text: Budh, Mercury, is linked in Jyotish with speech, intellect, learning, trade and communication. Its day is Wednesday (Budhvar). Commonly given colours are green; the metal is bronze or brass in many lists; the grain is green gram (moong); the gem is emerald (panna). Vishnu is the deity commonly connected to Budh, and many families also worship Ganesha on Wednesdays as the deity of beginnings and wisdom. Lists differ between regions and astrologers.

title: Budh worship practices and beej mantra
text: On Wednesdays many devotees worship Ganesha, offering durva grass and modak, and some wear green. Others recite Vishnu Sahasranama or give green moong to those in need. The beej mantra commonly given for Budh is "Om Braam Breem Braum Sah Budhaya Namah". Students sometimes keep Wednesday as a day for prayers before study. Practice varies by region and family.

title: Guru or Brihaspati (Jupiter) in Vedic astrology
text: Guru, also called Brihaspati, is Jupiter in Jyotish. He is linked with wisdom, teachers, knowledge, dharma and good fortune, and is regarded as the guru of the devas. Its day is Thursday (Guruvar or Brihaspativar). Commonly given colours are yellow and saffron; the metal is gold; the grain is chana dal (split Bengal gram); the gem is yellow sapphire (pukhraj). Vishnu is the deity most often linked with Thursday, and in some traditions Dattatreya or Brihaspati himself. Associations vary between sources.

title: Guru worship practices and beej mantra
text: On Thursdays many families observe Brihaspati vrat, wear yellow, offer yellow flowers, chana dal and bananas, and worship Vishnu or Lakshmi-Narayan. Some read the Brihaspati Vrat Katha. In many homes people avoid washing hair or cutting nails on this day, a custom that varies by region. The beej mantra commonly given for Guru is "Om Graam Greem Graum Sah Gurave Namah". Respecting teachers is also considered part of Guru worship.

title: Shukra (Venus) in Vedic astrology
text: Shukra, Venus, is linked in Jyotish with love, beauty, the arts, comfort, marriage and material prosperity. Its day is Friday (Shukravar). Commonly given colours are white, cream and soft pastels, with pink often used in practice; the metal is silver; the grain is rice or white beans in some lists; the gem is diamond (heera) or, as a traditional alternative, white sapphire or zircon. Lakshmi is the deity most commonly worshipped on Fridays, and Santoshi Maa is also worshipped on Fridays in North India. Associations vary.

title: Shukra and Friday worship practices
text: On Fridays many devotees worship Lakshmi, light lamps in the evening and keep the home clean, wearing white or light colours. Santoshi Maa vrat is kept on sixteen consecutive Fridays by many devotees, with a custom of avoiding sour foods. Others offer white sweets such as kheer. The beej mantra commonly given for Shukra is "Om Draam Dreem Draum Sah Shukraya Namah". Fasting customs differ by family and region.

title: Shani (Saturn) in Vedic astrology
text: Shani, Saturn, is linked in Jyotish with discipline, time, hard work, patience, service and the results of one's actions (karma). Its day is Saturday (Shanivar). Commonly given colours are black and dark blue; the metal is iron; the grains are sesame (til) and black gram (urad); the gem is blue sapphire (neelam), which astrologers usually advise treating with great caution. Shani Dev is the deity of the graha, and Hanuman is also worshipped on Saturdays in many parts of North India. Views differ among astrologers.

title: Shani worship practices and beej mantra
text: On Saturdays devotees commonly visit a Shani temple, offer mustard or sesame oil, black sesame and dark flowers, light a lamp under a peepal tree, or recite the Hanuman Chalisa. Some fast and wear black or dark blue. Charity to the poor, workers and the elderly is also a customary Saturday practice. The beej mantra commonly given is "Om Praam Preem Praum Sah Shanaischaraya Namah". Shani is respected as a teacher of discipline rather than feared, and practice varies by region.

title: Rahu in Vedic astrology
text: Rahu is one of the two shadow grahas (chhaya graha) in Jyotish. It is not a physical planet but the Moon's ascending node, treated as a graha. Rahu is linked with ambition, foreign matters, unconventional paths, technology and illusion (maya). It has no weekday of its own; instead a daily period called Rahu Kaal, which falls at a different time each day, is traditionally avoided for starting auspicious work in many regions. Commonly given colours are smoky blue, dark grey or black; the grain is black gram (urad); the gem is hessonite (gomed). Durga is the deity commonly connected with Rahu worship, and Shiva in some traditions.

title: Rahu worship practices and beej mantra
text: Customs linked to Rahu include worshipping Durga, especially on Tuesdays and Fridays, offering lamps at Rahu Kaal in some South Indian temples, and giving black gram or blue cloth in charity. The beej mantra commonly given is "Om Bhraam Bhreem Bhraum Sah Rahave Namah". The legend behind Rahu comes from the Puranic story of the churning of the ocean, where a demon drank the nectar of immortality and was severed by Vishnu. Practices differ widely and none is considered compulsory.

title: Ketu in Vedic astrology
text: Ketu is the second shadow graha, the Moon's descending node. In Jyotish it is linked with detachment, spiritual insight, moksha (liberation) and past-life tendencies, and is described as the headless counterpart of Rahu. It has no weekday of its own. Commonly given colours are grey, brown or multicoloured; the grain is horse gram (kulthi); the gem is cat's eye (lehsunia). Ganesha is the deity most often linked with Ketu worship, and in some traditions Bhairava or Shiva. Associations vary between lineages.

title: Ketu worship practices and beej mantra
text: Customs linked to Ketu include worshipping Ganesha, feeding dogs, visiting temples with a spiritual focus, and giving blankets or sesame in charity. The beej mantra commonly given is "Om Sraam Sreem Sraum Sah Ketave Namah". In the Puranic story, Rahu and Ketu are the two halves of the same demon; Ketu is the body and Rahu is the head. Practices differ between regions and families, and none is considered required.

title: Navagraha shrine and circumambulation custom
text: Many temples, especially in South India, have a Navagraha shrine where the nine grahas stand on a platform, with Surya in the centre and the others around him. Devotees often walk around it (parikrama) an odd number of times, commonly nine, reciting the beej mantras or offering lamps. Some Tamil Nadu pilgrims visit a circuit of nine temples near Kumbakonam, each linked to one graha. Customs differ by temple, and each temple's priest is the right guide for local practice.

title: Gemstones and the grahas, a traditional note
text: Jyotish traditionally links each graha with a gem: ruby for Surya, pearl for Chandra, red coral for Mangal, emerald for Budh, yellow sapphire for Guru, diamond for Shukra, blue sapphire for Shani, hessonite for Rahu, and cat's eye for Ketu. Astrologers generally advise consulting a knowledgeable person before wearing any gem, since opinions on suitability differ. Gems are a matter of personal belief and are not a substitute for professional advice, so Pandit ji may mention the tradition but should not recommend buying a stone.

title: What a puja is, and the sankalp
text: A puja is a ritual of worship in which a deity is honoured with offerings such as flowers, lamps, incense, water, fruit and sweets. A full puja is traditionally described as having sixteen offerings (shodashopachara), though simpler forms are common. It usually begins with a sankalp, a spoken statement of intent that names the worshipper, family lineage (gotra), place and date, and the purpose of the prayer. Pujas are devotional acts, and families decide for themselves how simple or elaborate they wish them to be.

title: What a havan or homa is
text: A havan, also called a homa or yajna, is a fire ritual in which ghee, grains, herbs and wood are offered into a consecrated fire (Agni) while mantras are chanted, with the word "swaha" at each offering. In tradition, Agni carries the offerings to the deities. Havans are performed at weddings, housewarmings, festivals and for specific deities such as Navagraha or Durga. Different woods and materials are prescribed for different purposes, and a qualified priest usually conducts them.

title: Muhurat, the auspicious time for a puja
text: A muhurat is a time considered auspicious for beginning a ceremony, worked out by a priest from the panchang (Hindu almanac), which uses the lunar day (tithi), weekday, star (nakshatra) and other factors. Weddings, Griha Pravesh and major pujas are usually fixed by muhurat. Panchang calculations vary slightly between regions, so a local pandit's date is the one to follow. A simple puja at home can be done any day, and many families treat the muhurat as helpful rather than essential.

title: Rudrabhishek
text: Rudrabhishek is a ritual bathing (abhishek) of the Shivling, in which water, milk, curd, honey, ghee, sugar and other substances are poured while the Sri Rudram hymn from the Yajurveda is chanted. The Shiva Purana praises the abhishek of Shiva. It is traditionally performed on Mondays, Pradosh, Maha Shivaratri and in the month of Shravan, and by families at temples such as Mahakaleshwar or Kashi Vishwanath. Devotees offer it as an act of devotion, and the format varies by region and temple.

title: Satyanarayan Puja and Katha
text: The Satyanarayan Puja honours Vishnu as the lord of truth (Satya-Narayan). It includes a reading of a katha, a story in five chapters, traditionally attributed to the Skanda Purana, about devotees who kept faith in the vrat. It is performed on Purnima, on Thursdays, and at occasions such as a new home, a wedding or a new business, mainly in North, Western and Eastern India. The prasad is a sweet made from semolina, ghee, sugar and banana, often with panchamrit. Practice varies between regions.

title: Navagraha Shanti Puja and Homa
text: The Navagraha Shanti puja worships all nine grahas, usually with a homa in which each graha receives its own mantra and its traditional wood: arka for Surya, palasha for Chandra, khadira for Mangal, apamarga for Budh, peepal for Guru, udumbara (fig) for Shukra, shami for Shani, durva grass for Rahu and kusha grass for Ketu. Families may arrange it before a new venture, at Griha Pravesh, on a birthday or when an astrologer suggests it. Shanti means "peace", and the ritual is a prayer for harmony rather than a promise of any outcome.

title: Shani Shanti and Tailabhishek
text: Shani Shanti puja is a prayer to Shani Dev, often done on Saturdays or Shani Amavasya. In Tailabhishek, sesame or mustard oil is poured on the Shani idol or stone while mantras are chanted, with black sesame, dark flowers and blue cloth as offerings. The Shani Stotra and Hanuman Chalisa may be recited. Many devotees perform it during Sade Sati or when an astrologer suggests it, as a customary way of showing respect to Shani. Temples such as Shani Shingnapur and Thirunallar are well-known centres.

title: Mangal Shanti or Mangal Dosha puja
text: The Mangal Shanti puja is a prayer to Mangal (Mars), often done on Tuesdays, sometimes at the Mangalnath temple in Ujjain, which tradition regards as the birthplace of Mangal. It may include a homa, red lentils, red cloth and the recitation of Mangal mantras or the Hanuman Chalisa. Families sometimes arrange it when a horoscope is said to show Mangal Dosha. In some regions a symbolic ritual called Kumbh Vivah is also done before a wedding. Astrologers differ in how much weight they give these customs.

title: Kaal Sarp Dosh puja
text: Kaal Sarp Dosh puja is a prayer performed when an astrologer notes that a horoscope has all planets between Rahu and Ketu. It is commonly done at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik, and at places like Ujjain, Srikalahasti and Prayagraj, with worship of Shiva and of the serpent deities (Nag). Devotees often do it on Nag Panchami or on certain new moon days. The idea of Kaal Sarp Dosh is not found in the older classical texts such as Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra, and astrologers disagree about it.

title: Pitra Tarpan and Shraddha, honouring ancestors
text: Shraddha is the Hindu rite of remembering and honouring one's ancestors (pitras) with food, water offerings (tarpan) and prayers, performed on the death anniversary and during Pitru Paksha, a fortnight in the lunar month of Bhadrapada or Ashwin. The final day, Sarva Pitru Amavasya, is used for all ancestors. Pind daan is done at places like Gaya, Varanasi and Haridwar. Families feed Brahmins, cows, crows and dogs, and give to the needy. At its heart the rite is gratitude and remembrance, and customs vary by community.

title: Maha Mrityunjaya Jaap
text: The Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra ("Om Tryambakam Yajamahe ...") is a Vedic prayer to Shiva that appears in the Rigveda and is widely used in the Shiva tradition. A jaap, repeated chanting, is commonly done 108 times a day, or in larger counts by priests over several days. Devotees recite it with prayers for the health and wellbeing of a named person or family. It is a prayer and a devotional practice, and not a substitute for medical care. It is often chanted on Mondays or during Shravan.

title: Lakshmi Puja
text: Lakshmi Puja is performed at home on Fridays by many families, and on the new moon night of Diwali, when Lakshmi is worshipped along with Ganesha, often at the Pradosh time in the evening. Homes are cleaned, lit with diyas and decorated with rangoli. Offerings include lotus or red flowers, sweets, coins and the Sri Suktam or Lakshmi Ashtottara may be recited. Business families perform Chopda Pujan, worshipping new account books. Customs vary by region.

title: Ganesh Puja
text: Ganesh Puja is the worship of Ganesha, and in Hindu custom he is invoked first at the start of any ceremony, wedding or new venture. It is performed on Wednesdays, Chaturthi days and above all at Ganesh Chaturthi, when clay idols are installed for a number of days and later immersed. Offerings include modak, durva grass and red hibiscus, and the Ganapati Atharvashirsha may be recited. In Maharashtra and many parts of India it is also a community festival.

title: Sundarkand Path
text: Sundarkand is the fifth book of the Valmiki Ramayana and also of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, telling of Hanuman's journey to Lanka and his meeting with Sita. A Sundarkand Path is a recitation of this book, commonly in the Tulsidas version in North India, often over one sitting and with a kalash and lamp. Devotees do it on Tuesdays and Saturdays, at a new home, or at family gatherings. It is a devotional reading, and groups sometimes sing it together with music.

title: Hanuman Chalisa Path
text: The Hanuman Chalisa is a forty-verse hymn to Hanuman written by Tulsidas in Awadhi. Many devotees recite it daily, and on Tuesdays and Saturdays in particular; some read it 11 or 108 times at special occasions such as Hanuman Jayanti or before a new venture. It can be done at home, in a temple or in a group (satsang), with a lamp lit before an image of Hanuman. It is a devotional practice, and families differ in how many repetitions they choose.

title: Durga Saptashati Path
text: The Durga Saptashati, also called the Devi Mahatmya or Chandi Path, has about seven hundred verses in thirteen chapters and is part of the Markandeya Purana. It is read especially during Navratri, either in full or a few chapters each day, often preceded by the Kavach, Argala and Keelak stotras. Many families have it recited by a priest and conclude with a havan on Ashtami or Navami. It is a devotional text of the Goddess, and the format differs between Shakta traditions.

title: Griha Pravesh, the housewarming ceremony
text: Griha Pravesh is the ceremony for first entering a new home. A priest sets an auspicious date, and the family usually enters with a kalash, a lamp and Ganesha worship, followed by a Vastu or Navagraha puja and often a Satyanarayan Katha. In many North Indian families milk is boiled over a stove until it overflows, as a sign of abundance, and the doorway is decorated with a mango-leaf toran and rangoli. Customs differ by region, and the date is chosen from the panchang.

title: Om (Aum), the sacred syllable
text: Om (also written Aum) is the sacred syllable of Hindu tradition. The Mandukya Upanishad explains it as made of the sounds A, U and M, plus the silence after them, and devotees read these as waking, dreaming and deep sleep, with silence as the fourth state beyond them. Om begins most mantras and prayers and is written in Devanagari as a shape like a numeral 3 with a curl, a crescent and a dot. It is linked to no single deity or weekday and is used by Hindus, Buddhists and Jains in their own ways.

title: How Om is used in worship and design
text: Om is chanted at the start of prayer, yoga and meditation, drawn at the entrance of homes and temples, and worn as a pendant. Because it is regarded as sacred, many devotees prefer that Om appears with respect, for example not on footwear or places considered unclean. A designer or wearer may choose an Om with a lotus, a sun, or a mandala. It is suitable on any day, though some devotees link it with Sunday and the Sun as the source of light.

title: The swastika in Hinduism, an auspicious symbol
text: The swastika (from Sanskrit "svasti", well-being) is an ancient auspicious symbol in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, used for thousands of years in India. Hindus draw it, often in red kumkum, at doorways, on new account books at Diwali, at weddings and at Griha Pravesh. Its four arms are read as the four directions, four Vedas or four aims of life (purusharthas). It is closely associated with Ganesha and Lakshmi. It is distinct from the tilted emblem adopted by the Nazi party in the twentieth century, so context should always be explained to avoid misunderstanding.

title: Trishul, Shiva's trident
text: The trishul is the three-pronged trident carried by Shiva and also by Durga in many images. Devotees read the three prongs in different ways, such as creation, preservation and destruction, or past, present and future, or the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas). The damru is often tied to it. It is linked to Monday, Mahashivaratri and Shiva worship in general. Interpretations differ between schools, and the symbol is popular in devotional art and on T-shirts for devotees of Shiva.

title: Damru, Shiva's drum
text: The damru is the small hourglass-shaped drum held by Shiva, especially in his Nataraja form. Tradition links its sound with the rhythm of creation and with the origin of Sanskrit, since the Maheshwara Sutras, a list of the Sanskrit sound groups, are traditionally said to have come from its beats. The drum is shown in Shiva's hand along with the trishul. It is associated with Monday and Shiva worship and is a popular motif in temple art and devotional designs.

title: Shankh, the conch
text: The shankh (conch shell) is carried by Vishnu, and Krishna's conch Panchajanya is blown in the Mahabharata. Blowing a conch begins many Hindu ceremonies, aartis and temple rituals, and its sound is considered auspicious. In the Mahabharata, conches announce the start of the Kurukshetra war. The shankh is also kept in many home shrines and is linked with Lakshmi, who rose from the ocean as the conch did, in popular tradition. It relates to Vishnu worship and Thursday.

title: Sudarshan Chakra, Vishnu's discus
text: The Sudarshan Chakra is the spinning discus with serrated edges that Vishnu holds in one hand. Devotees read it as the wheel of time and of dharma, a symbol of protection and of righteous power. Krishna is also shown with the Sudarshan Chakra in many stories. It is a major motif in Vaishnava art and the emblem of the Sri Vaishnava tradition, shown on flags and temple pillars. It is linked to Vishnu worship and Thursday, and to Ekadashi.

title: Padma, the lotus
text: The lotus (padma) grows from mud yet rises clean, so it is read as purity, spiritual unfolding and detachment. Lakshmi sits on a lotus, Saraswati sits on a white lotus, Vishnu holds a lotus, and Brahma is born from one at Vishnu's navel. The lotus is also the basis of chakra imagery. It is linked with Friday and Lakshmi worship, and with the colours white and pink. The lotus is India's national flower and a common motif in Hindu art and designs.

title: Kalash, the sacred pot
text: The kalash is a pot filled with water, topped with mango leaves and a coconut, and is placed at the start of many pujas, weddings and Griha Pravesh ceremonies. It is read as a symbol of abundance and as the seat of the deities invoked, and is linked to the churning of the ocean and the pot of nectar. It is closely associated with Lakshmi and Varuna, and appears in Navratri Ghatasthapana. Decorations on it, such as kumkum, a swastika and a red thread, vary by region.

title: Sri Yantra, structure and meaning
text: The Sri Yantra, also called Sri Chakra, is a diagram of nine interlocking triangles, four pointing upward and five pointing downward, forming forty-three smaller triangles, surrounded by two rings of lotus petals and a square gateway (bhupura). Tradition links the upward triangles with Shiva and the downward ones with Shakti, meeting at the central point (bindu). It is the principal yantra of Sri Vidya, the Tripura Sundari tradition, and in popular practice is also associated with Lakshmi, prosperity and Friday. Its use in worship is guided by lineage teachers.

title: Sri Yantra in homes and on art
text: Many homes and shops keep a Sri Yantra, often in metal, as a sacred diagram, and some devotees worship it on Fridays or during Navratri and Diwali. Customs for worship differ, and traditional Sri Vidya sources say the formal practice should be learned from a teacher. As a design on a T-shirt it is a geometric symbol of the Goddess, and the wearer can enjoy it without any promise of results.

title: Navagraha Yantra or mandala
text: A Navagraha yantra or mandala is a diagram that places the nine grahas together, often in a three-by-three grid with Surya in the centre, or in a circular arrangement with each graha's colour. Temples with Navagraha shrines use a similar layout. Devotees worship it to honour all nine grahas at once, for example during Navagraha puja or a graha shanti. The colours follow the commonly given scheme for each graha, which differs by region. It is a devotional diagram, and lineage teachers may give differing layouts.

title: Hanuman Yantra
text: The Hanuman Yantra is a geometric diagram, often a hexagram or square with bija syllables and the name of Hanuman, worshipped in some traditions along with the Hanuman Chalisa. Devotees keep it at home or in a shop, and it is usually associated with Tuesday and Saturday and with the colours red and orange. Its exact design differs between texts and lineages, so no single form is standard. As a design on a T-shirt it is a symbol of Hanuman's strength and devotion.

title: Ganesha Yantra
text: The Ganesha Yantra is a geometric diagram, usually triangle- or lotus-based, with the seed syllable "Gam" and the name of Ganesha. Devotees worship it in some traditions at the start of new ventures, on Wednesdays and on Ganesh Chaturthi. Its exact form varies between texts and lineages. As a design it combines sacred geometry with the beloved elephant-headed deity, and is read as a symbol of auspicious beginnings and obstacles being removed, as tradition describes.

title: What a yantra is
text: A yantra is a geometric diagram used in Tantric and devotional practice as a seat for a deity or as an object of meditation. It is typically made of triangles, circles, lotus petals and a square frame, with a central point (bindu), and sometimes with seed syllables. Different deities have different yantras. Traditional use includes consecration (prana pratishtha) and mantra recitation under guidance. A yantra on a T-shirt is a design inspired by sacred geometry and does not substitute for such practice.

title: Mandala in Hindu tradition
text: A mandala (Sanskrit for circle) is a circular, symmetrical diagram that represents the cosmos or the seat of a deity, with a central point from which the design radiates outward. Mandalas appear in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions, with different meanings in each. In Hindu worship, temple floors, rangoli and diagrams drawn for pujas use mandala forms, and the Navagraha mandala and Sri Yantra are examples. In design, a mandala is often used as a calming, meditative motif with lotus petals or deity symbols at the centre.

title: Gada, the mace
text: The gada (mace) is a heavy club carried by Hanuman, by Vishnu (as Kaumodaki) and by Bhima in the Mahabharata. It is read by devotees as strength used in service of dharma. In Hanuman imagery it is a defining feature, along with red or saffron colour. It is related to Tuesday and Saturday worship of Hanuman and to wrestlers' akhadas, where Hanuman is the patron. It is a popular motif in designs of Hanuman and Vishnu.

title: Rudraksha beads
text: Rudraksha are the seeds of a tree, worn or used as a mala (prayer-bead string) by devotees of Shiva. The name means "eye of Rudra", and tradition, including the Shiva Purana, tells of beads born from Shiva's tears. Beads are classed by their natural lines, called mukhi, with the five-faced bead most common, and traditional texts attribute different meanings to each. A 108-bead rudraksha mala is used to count mantras such as "Om Namah Shivaya". Beliefs about each type vary, and the beads are devotional items.

title: Diya, the oil lamp
text: The diya is an oil or ghee lamp lit in nearly every Hindu puja. It is read as the light of knowledge removing darkness, which is the meaning behind Diwali, the festival of lights. Ghee lamps are commonly offered to Vishnu and Lakshmi, and sesame or mustard oil lamps to Shani in many customs. Lighting a lamp at dawn or dusk in front of the home shrine is a widely followed daily practice. Its form varies from clay diyas to large brass temple lamps.

title: Peacock feather (mor pankh)
text: The peacock feather is a signature element of Krishna's crown and is used in devotional art, home shrines and decoration. It is also linked with Kartikeya, whose vahana is the peacock, and with Saraswati in some depictions. Devotees read the many colours of the feather as the richness of creation. The peacock is India's national bird. The feather is a popular T-shirt motif for devotees of Krishna, and has no fixed weekday.

title: How the seven weekdays link to grahas and deities
text: In Hindu tradition each weekday (vara) is linked to a graha, and by custom to one or more deities: Sunday to Surya, Monday to Chandra and Shiva, Tuesday to Mangal and Hanuman, Wednesday to Budh and Vishnu or Ganesha, Thursday to Guru and Vishnu, Friday to Shukra and Lakshmi or Devi, Saturday to Shani and Hanuman. The pairings of deity with day are popular custom and differ between regions and families. A vrat is a vow or fast kept on a chosen day; it is optional and personal.

title: Why a design is suggested for a weekday
text: When Pandit ji suggests a T-shirt design for a weekday, it is a style idea built on the traditional day-deity pairings, for example a Hanuman design for Tuesday or a Lakshmi design for Friday. It is not a ritual requirement, and wearing a design does not replace worship or carry any promised result. Colours suggested follow commonly given customs, which differ by region. Devotees may simply enjoy wearing the symbols and colours of the deity they feel close to, on any day.

title: Sunday (Ravivar): Surya's day
text: Sunday (Ravivar or Adityavar) is the day of Surya, the Sun. Commonly linked colours are red, orange and saffron. Surya is worshipped by offering water at sunrise and reciting Surya mantras or the Aditya Hridayam. In some regions Sunday is also associated with Surya-linked forms such as Suryanarayana, and with Bhairava in a few traditions. The graha-day link comes from Jyotish, while the deity pairings vary by community.

title: Sunday vrat customs
text: Devotees who keep a Sunday vrat for Surya often rise before sunrise, bathe, offer water to the Sun and eat only one meal, commonly without salt, after sunset or in the afternoon. Many read the Ravivar Vrat Katha. Wearing red or orange is customary. Some tie the fast to a set number of Sundays, such as twelve. Customs vary by family, and anyone with health needs should adapt a fast sensibly.

title: Design ideas for Sunday
text: For Sunday, a design inspired by Surya fits the tradition: a radiant sun, a sun mandala, the seven-horse chariot of Surya, or an Om with sun rays. Saffron, orange, red or copper tones follow the commonly given colours for the day. The seven horses are often read as the seven days or the seven colours of light. These are style suggestions based on custom, not a ritual requirement.

title: Monday (Somvar): Shiva and Chandra's day
text: Monday (Somvar) is the day of Chandra, the Moon, and is widely observed as Shiva's day, since Shiva wears the crescent moon on his head and is called Somanath or Chandrashekhar. Commonly worn colours are white and cream. Devotees offer water, milk, bael leaves (bilva patra) and white flowers to the Shivling. The Shravan month Mondays are especially observed. Observance is optional and varies by region.

title: Somvar vrat customs
text: Many devotees keep a Monday fast (Somvar vrat) for Shiva, taking one meal or fruits and milk, visiting a Shiva temple and reciting "Om Namah Shivaya". Some keep sixteen Mondays (Solah Somvar), a custom popular in parts of North and Western India, and the Somvar Vrat Katha is read. Many wear white. Customs differ by family; the fast is a personal choice and does not require elaborate arrangements.

title: Design ideas for Monday
text: For Monday, designs linked to Shiva follow the tradition: the trishul, the damru, a crescent moon, the Shivling, Nandi the bull, or "Om Namah Shivaya" in Devanagari. White, cream, light grey or soft blue tones follow the commonly given colours for the day. Shiva imagery is popular year-round and is not limited to Mondays. These are style suggestions, not a ritual requirement.

title: Tuesday (Mangalvar): Hanuman and Mangal's day
text: Tuesday (Mangalvar) is the day of Mangal, Mars. In North India it is widely observed as Hanuman's day, and in South India Tuesdays are also kept for Kartikeya (Murugan) and for the Goddess. Commonly worn colours are red, vermilion and orange. Devotees visit Hanuman temples, offer sindoor, red flowers and boondi or laddus, and recite the Hanuman Chalisa. Saturday is the other day many families give to Hanuman.

title: Mangalvar vrat customs
text: The Mangalvar vrat is kept by many devotees for Hanuman: one meal a day, commonly without salt, often wheat or jaggery-based foods, with a visit to a Hanuman temple in the evening. Reciting the Hanuman Chalisa or Sundarkand is customary. Some keep twenty-one Tuesdays. In some families the fast is also linked to Mangal. Customs differ widely, and many people simply visit the temple without fasting.

title: Design ideas for Tuesday
text: For Tuesday, a Hanuman design follows the tradition: Hanuman with the gada (mace), Hanuman carrying the mountain, Hanuman revealing Ram in his heart, or a Hanuman Yantra. Red, orange and vermilion follow the commonly given colours. Designers might also use the Devanagari "Jai Shri Hanuman" or the Mangal beej mantra. These are style suggestions, not a ritual requirement, and Hanuman designs are equally suitable on Saturdays or any day.

title: Wednesday (Budhvar): Budh, Ganesha and Vishnu
text: Wednesday (Budhvar) is the day of Budh, Mercury. By popular custom it is widely observed for Ganesha, the remover of obstacles and patron of learning, and some families also worship Vishnu or Krishna. Commonly worn colours are green. Devotees offer durva grass and modak to Ganesha. Observance varies by community.

title: Budhvar vrat customs
text: Some families keep a Wednesday fast (Budhvar vrat), often a single meal with green foods such as moong dal, and read the Budhvar Vrat Katha. Others simply visit a Ganesha temple. Green clothing or green offerings are customary in many homes. The Wednesday fast is less widely kept than Monday, Thursday or Saturday fasts, and practice depends on family and region.

title: Design ideas for Wednesday
text: For Wednesday, a Ganesha design follows common custom: Ganesha with his modak, the mooshak (mouse) vahana, a single-line Ganesha, or a Ganesha Yantra. Green follows the commonly given colour for Budh, while red and orange are also popular for Ganesha. Designers might add "Om Gan Ganapataye Namah" in Devanagari. These are style suggestions, not a ritual requirement, and Ganesha designs suit any day.

title: Thursday (Guruvar): Guru and Vishnu's day
text: Thursday (Guruvar or Brihaspativar) is the day of Guru, Jupiter, and is widely associated with Vishnu and Lakshmi-Narayan. It is also a day for honouring teachers; in many traditions it is observed for Dattatreya, and in modern popular practice many devotees visit temples of Sai Baba of Shirdi on Thursdays. Commonly worn colours are yellow and saffron. Practice varies a great deal between communities.

title: Brihaspativar vrat customs
text: The Brihaspativar (Guruvar) vrat is kept by many families: one meal, commonly yellow foods such as chana dal and banana, worship of Vishnu or Brihaspati, and reading of the Brihaspati Vrat Katha. Devotees often wear yellow and offer yellow flowers. Some keep sixteen Thursdays. In many homes the banana tree is worshipped on this day. Customs vary, and the fast is a personal choice.

title: Design ideas for Thursday
text: For Thursday, designs linked to Vishnu follow the tradition: the Sudarshan Chakra, shankh (conch), padma (lotus), Vishnu on Sheshnag, Lakshmi-Narayan together, or the Devanagari "Om Namo Narayanaya". Yellow, saffron and gold tones follow the commonly given colours. Designs of a guru or the Om can also suit a day for teachers. These are style suggestions, not a ritual requirement.

title: Friday (Shukravar): Lakshmi, Devi and Shukra
text: Friday (Shukravar) is the day of Shukra, Venus, and is widely observed as the day of Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity. In many regions it is also the day of Santoshi Maa, of Durga, and of other forms of the Goddess; Friday evenings are a favourite time for Devi temples. Commonly worn colours are white, cream or pastel, while red, pink and gold are popular for Lakshmi and Devi. Practice varies by region.

title: Shukravar vrat and Santoshi Maa customs
text: On Fridays many devotees worship Lakshmi, light a lamp in the evening and keep the home clean. The Santoshi Maa vrat, which became widely popular in the second half of the twentieth century, is kept on sixteen Fridays by many women, with jaggery and roasted gram (chana) as the prasad and a custom of avoiding sour foods. The Shukravar Vrat Katha is read. Customs differ by family and region.

title: Design ideas for Friday
text: For Friday, designs linked to Lakshmi follow the tradition: Lakshmi seated on a lotus, the padma (lotus), the kalash with coconut, the Sri Yantra, or lamps (diyas). White, cream, pink, red and gold follow the commonly given or popular colours. A Santoshi Maa or Durga design also fits Fridays in many regions. These are style suggestions, not a ritual requirement.

title: Saturday (Shanivar): Shani Dev and Hanuman
text: Saturday (Shanivar) is the day of Shani, Saturn. Shani Dev is worshipped at dedicated temples, and in North India Hanuman is also worshipped on Saturdays; a well-known Puranic story, retold in popular tradition, links the two. In the South, Saturdays are also observed for Venkateswara (Balaji) in some families. Commonly worn colours are black and dark blue. Practice varies between regions.

title: Shanivar vrat customs
text: The Shanivar vrat is kept by many devotees: one meal, often without salt, avoiding oil-fried food, and a visit to a Shani or Hanuman temple. Mustard or sesame oil, black sesame and black cloth are common offerings. Many give food or clothes to the needy. Reading the Hanuman Chalisa is customary on this day. Some keep seven or eleven Saturdays. Customs vary, and the fast is a personal choice.

title: Design ideas for Saturday
text: For Saturday, designs linked to Shani Dev or Hanuman follow the tradition: Shani Dev on his crow or vulture, the Shani beej mantra in Devanagari, Hanuman with a gada, or a Hanuman Yantra. Black, dark blue and indigo follow the commonly given colours for the day. These are style suggestions based on custom, not a ritual requirement, and any deity design may be worn on any day.

title: Rahu Kaal, a daily period
text: Rahu Kaal is a period of about ninety minutes each day, calculated from sunrise and sunset, and it falls at a different time on each weekday. In many regions, especially South India, families avoid starting new ventures or ceremonies during it, while worship and prayers are generally still done. Some almanacs (panchang) publish the timings daily. Not everyone observes it, and traditions differ about how strictly.

title: What a vrat is, and sensible observance
text: A vrat is a vow taken for devotion and self-discipline, often involving a fast, prayer and a katha (story) reading. Fasts range from complete abstinence to a single meal, fruits or milk, and vary by family. Tradition itself permits adjusting a fast for age, illness, pregnancy or work, and many teachers say sincerity and kindness matter more than strictness. Anyone with a health condition should follow medical advice first. A vrat is a devotional practice, not a transaction.
